Apparently since people complained about how easy Normal mode was they added Hard mode, and of course I was one of them.

Hard mode? Makes you deal 1/15 HP damaged with a maxed out end game character from the base game in the DLC, and enemies kill you in 2-3 hits. So make normal mode piss easy and then make Hard Mode the most tedious and poorly designed difficulty ever conceived where you have zero opportunities to reliably kill enemies and therefor grind. 

For reference I tried the Trials at first and thought maybe I needed to try the DLC first instead? Nope, same issue. Apparently, when Hard mode said 'Seasoned Adventurer's' what they meant to say is 'Please make sure you are level 300 and have minmaxed relics and character before starting'. Oh want to change back? Sorry, better restart the entire game. 

I have no issue with wanting difficulty. I take issue with making every mob encounter a tedious 'spam your weapon ability constantly while enemies never stagger' fest, even with Dragonforged Dwavern enhanced base end game gear and being level 120. Why even bother releasing this when it actively penalizes players who already beat the end game on normal difficulty? 

If I could refund this garbage I would. Apparently Crapcom have no idea how to actually design difficulty in a game, evidenced by handing out the Eternal Ferrystone to all players rather than making it a reward to earn naturally or given on NG+ once the exploration has worn out it's welcome.

**A slap in the face to the people who supported this game from day one.**

I bought Dragon’s Dogma 2 at launch because I believed in the game and wanted to support the developers. Like many other early adopters, I had to put up with a game plagued by bugs, performance issues, and numerous problems that required subsequent updates to address.

Now, with the release of the DLC, new players can purchase the base game and the complete package at a much more attractive price, while those of us who supported the game from day one are left paying full price for the new content.

Where is the appreciation for the people who supported you when the game was at its most problematic?

We were there from the beginning. We paid full price, endured the technical issues, and trusted you to improve the experience. Our support helped establish the foundation for the game's continued development. Yet now, the people who waited on the sidelines, watched the game improve, and avoided the risks that early adopters had to take are being offered a better deal.

I'm not saying new players don't deserve a good deal. They absolutely do. But why can't you offer them an attractive package while also giving existing owners a loyalty discount? Why must attracting new customers come at the expense of acknowledging the people who supported you first?

A simple discount for existing owners would have shown that you value your most loyal customers. Instead, this pricing strategy makes early adopters feel like their support was only important when you needed their money.

It's not just about the DLC. It's about respect, trust, and appreciation. We took a chance on your game at launch, when it was far from perfect, and now it feels like that loyalty means absolutely nothing.

Why should we continue supporting games on day one, trusting developers, and putting up with launch problems if waiting is ultimately rewarded while early supporters receive no meaningful recognition?

**This is incredibly disappointing. If this is how you treat the people who supported you from the beginning, don't be surprised when they decide to wait for the next game to go on sale instead of buying it at launch.**

I had a great time with this game back in 2024 but, as everyone knows, it wasn't exempt of heavy criticism for good reason. At the time I even thought Capcom let the game be a tech demo based on what they were aiming to do in MH Wilds but unfortunately not much was learned from this during Wilds' release.

Performance was really rough, especially in Vernworth and Bakhbattahl, and there was also the double whammy of Dragonsplague being a thing so sleeping away from settlements was much more preferred just in case one of your pawns had it bc if one of them went rampant, there was a chance of your save getting softlocked if a quest giver died during that rampage...there were more mind-boggling decisions like the whole MTX drama that blew out of proportion, having the same 9 enemies all around, the refusal of granting everyone an Eternal Ferrystone bc it was "Itsuno's vision" to have us wander back and forth between places without fast travel, repeating the same issue from DD1 vanilla giving us only one save file and so on...

DD2 vanilla was fun but...it was also super rough.

However, as time went on, Itsuno left the company and the game remained in a somewhat playable state until the past couple of months where many performance and QoL changes have been applied that have made DD2 have a much better experience now that I came back in preparation for the DLC. 

The story is still a bit barebones and it only gets better during the final hours but it's still better than the story from DD1 vanilla. The combat is where this game truly shines bc no other game in the genre has the sauce this one has for their classes/vocations and that'd be the biggest reason I'd ask everyone to give DD2 a try.

Pre-Expansion re-review. 
Game's good. I started a new playthrough to get the feel of the game again rather than continuing my old playthrough. 
Performance: The game is FAR more stable now in frame rate and consistency, though NPC pop in is still atrocious in cities. I do rarely get a crash but the auto saves are pretty generous, I haven't lost any meaningful progress. 
Combat: Still as it was, feels fantastic and weighty and the two extra combat abilities add a lot to your playstyle. Hopefully expansion hard mode will be good for people that want a bigger challenge, guess we'll find out soon.
Exploration: Wonderful, still wish we got more enemy variety but the expansion will hopefully partially address that. Infinite ferrystone like the one we had in DD1 does 'cheapen' the adventure vibe a bit, but really it's not mandatory and anyone claiming otherwise is a moron. Wanna zip around your network of portcrystals? You can do it now without restriction. Wanna hoof it? You can do that too. 
The story: I wish they touched it up to at least flow better. It's still hot garbage, a genuine dumpster fire of a fantasy story at best, being forced to listen to Raghnall's voice acting at worst. Don't expect any improvements here. Nothing DD2 offers compares even slightly to the hype of DD1 Grigori jumping in, throwing the plot in the trash and saying 'let's fight bro'. But that's okay because we have a skip button.
Only real con: I wish we could filter pawns by active players so we could support each other a bit more easily. Going to discord servers or whatever social media of your  choice to find people's pawns to summon sucks. 

TLDR
Is good. Go play.

The game now runs buttery smooth, and I can finally enjoy it at max resolution with high, stable FPS. I genuinely appreciate Capcom’s dedication and hard work in fixing these deep-rooted performance issues rather than abandoning them. Now that it runs as intended, Dragon's Dogma 2 is an incredible masterpiece and an absolute must-play for any adventure and action-RPG fan!

I finished the game on my old PC when it first released, and we all remember how bad the performance was back then. For me, it was basically a 30 FPS simulator inside the cities, sometimes dropping to 15 FPS, while outside the cities I could barely reach 60 FPS. Despite that, I finished the game and didn't want to play it again anytime soon.

Now I've come back to the game after all the updates, and what a difference. The updates fixed a ton of issues, including the optimization. On my current setup, with almost everything maxed out, I'm getting a stable 60–80 FPS inside cities, while outside the cities it basically never drops below 110 FPS. Obviously, I still have some settings turned down because they consume a ridiculous amount of resources without providing any noticeable visual benefit, but overall, the performance is massively better.

So, what's my review of the game?

The game gives you very little hand-holding when it comes to quests. Some quests actually require you to use your brain, read what NPCs are telling you, and pay attention to the world around you. If you don't feel like figuring everything out yourself, Google is probably going to become your best friend.

I also recommend getting some high-level Pawns. They can carry you through difficult combat encounters, but they can also be surprisingly useful when you're trying to figure out where to go or what to do during certain quests.

Fast travel exists. You have Ferrystones, and nowadays you get a permanent one, which makes things much more convenient. You can also obtain additional Ferrystones through quests or buy them from certain NPCs. Portcrystals can be obtained and placed in strategic locations, making traveling around the map much easier. On top of that, major cities and many villages already have permanent teleport locations, so the game actually does a pretty good job of making fast travel available for people who don't want to spend half their life walking across the map.

And if you're one of those people who doesn't want to "adventure through the world" every single time you need to go somewhere, there are also ox carts that can take you to many locations.

That said, you're still going to have to explore the world at least once. Whether you do it on foot or by cart is up to you.

Story-wise, it's difficult to say much without getting into spoilers. Generally speaking, the game feels like one of those isekai adventures you've probably watched once, twice, or maybe way too many times. You're thrown into a fantasy world, become increasingly powerful, meet a bunch of strange characters, and eventually get dragged into something much bigger than yourself.

The game also has a ton of different vocations. You have classic warriors with shields, mages capable of ridiculous power fantasies like dropping a meteor on enemies, and much more specialized classes.

Then there's the Warfarer, which is basically the "I'll do it myself" vocation. You can use skills from different vocations and combine them with the equipment you want, allowing you to build something that fits your own playstyle.

And if you're worried that some vocations might be overpowered: honestly, almost every vocation can become completely broken if you understand how to play it and build around its strengths. The game absolutely rewards power fantasy, and when your character becomes powerful, you can really feel it.

Now, what about the in-game shop?

The microtransaction complaints were everywhere before and around release, so if that was something that put you off the game, it's worth clarifying that the things people complained about can be obtained through normal gameplay. You don't need to spend additional money to access them. You can simply play the game normally and enjoy it as intended.

Pawns are another major part of the game. Other players' Pawns can have personal quests if their owners have assigned them one, so it's worth checking them out. You can get some easy resources or money from these quests.

Personally, I also like giving my Pawn expensive items so that other players can either use them or sell them for a decent amount of gold. It's a small thing, but it's part of what makes the Pawn system interesting.

And finally, if you've already finished the game once, there is NG+, so you can go through the game again with your existing character and experience it in a way that feels a bit more like your own personal fantasy Monster Hunter.

Overall, Dragon's Dogma 2 is a game that I think is much easier to recommend now than it was at release. The performance problems were a huge part of my original experience, and coming back to it on a modern setup makes the difference absolutely massive.

If you like games that don't constantly tell you exactly what to do, give you a lot of freedom in how you build your character, and let you become ridiculously powerful when you understand the systems, it's definitely worth giving Dragon's Dogma 2 another look.

I remember the first time i beat Ashe and actually broke down into tears.
When i found out that that was just easy mode and now i got to experience the real thing, Something called Awakened Daimon. I cried even harder.
Not because it was going to be more difficult.
Because it meant i could still get stronger at the game.
Because it meant i got to experience what it felt like to walk up to a god and shake his hand not just once, but twice.
Because this time, that god wouldn't be pulling his punches.
That is what made it feel so good.
The experience was REAL.
They didn't hold your hand the first time you played through it and they certainly didn't start with the second run either.
You were always thrown into this dark abyss and told to crawl to the bottom without a light, But somehow they managed to make that genuinely harrowing experience into something you will honestly never forget.
It became the cornerstone for every real gamer at the time.
It became something you had every right to be proud of.
It meant you genuinely scratched your way into hell, Nails peeling, fingers bloodied, And stared into the face of a god that had been watching you grow the entire time.
That is exactly the kind of experience that current game development fails to capture time and time again and in my opinion they might never be able to even scratch the surface of.
All i want to say is i cant wait for this Dark Arisen DLC.
And i will F****** dominate it through every drop of blood, sweat and tear i have.

I want to like this game.
I feel like its a bunch of ideas, some of them actually pretty good, put together into something that resembles a game that was made by newer developers.
It has a lot of telling and not showing. Some things just conveniently happen for the story. Quests, the main story included, generally feel like bullet points. They needed to go back through and flesh them out and give them more meat. I didn't feel like I cared about what was happening most of the time. Which is sad since the general premise of the story is good.

(END TLDR)

Quests also have a hard time triggering at times, where I'd have to go back again the next day and walk slower into the area trigger. Or, surprise, an npc for the quest had died in a random attack and now the quest won't start at all until you go to the morgue, find the random npc who might have been with this quest, who had died, and revive him with one of your few precious wakestones. These stones are also used to revive you in combat if you die. They are limited and not common.
There are secret quests or secret quest objectives in this game that are on a timer. It doesn't explain it to you and some quests will just 'end', the quest will say complete and it will be removed from your quest log, but in reality, you have 3 days to talk to this random npc to continue the quest and get the 'good' ending for it. This would be one of those good ideas, but it is implemented poorly, not explained, and starts happening part way through the game on quests that 'matter' (matter in the sense of having actual stakes of some sort. In this case, an npc lives or dies depending on if you talk to this secret npc).

The game will also punish you at certain times for the vocation you are using. One example is when you get to Bakbatallh. When going down one of the ally ways you are 'challenged' by a group of thugs to fight. It's a 3 vs 1 fight that you are forced into since your pawns watch. If you are a mage class, then you are in for a rough time since they are all melee classes and will be on you like glue. Even with the stamina casting ability, which uses stamina to cast magic faster, you do not have enough time to cast anything before you get hit by any of these guys, which cancels your casting. (in this quest the fight turns into a 1v1 once you get to a certain point, but this type of thing happens a few times).
The Trickster class is also a good idea that is also terrible. It's a special class that only the Arisen can use and it is Agro the class. You cast a shade that has a health pool and enemies are agro'd onto it. That's the class. Against smaller groups of monsters it is actually a pretty interesting class, but you need most of the abilities in the class to feel effective since you do basically zero damage to anything and even with those abilities, you are trying to bait enemies to jump off cliffs, which your pawns and the AI will go out of their way to not let you do it. Half the illusions that you can cast the AI will ignore anyway.


Some good things though. The world itself looks good. While npcs were literally spawning right next to me and in front of me while walking through cities, exploring out in the wilderness was generally pretty fun. There are only 3 biomes in the game but they all felt distinct from each other and looked good.
Combat was good. Not great, but good enough. I feel like the melee classes are what you are 'supposed' to play as and I felt engaged while using them (I didn't use the bow classes in my play through). Magic does feel fun when you get it off against smaller enemies, but against bosses it just feels like you are spamming it to watch the huge bar go down.
Climbing in combat is fun but can get annoying against some bosses. Some will require you to climb them when you get them to critically low health, and if you don't do it fast enough, they will do an 'ult' ability on themselves and make you climb them again.
The Pawn system is also 'good'. I like having an npc that I create that follows me around the entire game, but can also go into other peoples worlds and help them. (I had my trusty Bob Ross, who was a fighter/warrior the entire game). You also can summon two other pawns from other's games to help you out (designs of characters vary from good to horrifying). This does make you have to swap out half your party constantly since the pawn you have is now to low of a level to help you in certain areas. If the pawn was present in a quest in their host world, or your pawn helped someone with a quest, then they will offer to help you in your world with that quest, or to find an item, etc. It's a cool concept but they will generally not shut up about it in game. Also, voice acting quality varies and there are not that many voices in game, so you hear a lot of the same voices over All characters. (Shout out to Sir Kruber and Sienna's voice actors from the Vermintide series.)

I have waited until I cleared mostly everything before I even dare to try and write a review. So, after completing the true ending and completing most of the quests (except for sorcerer/mage meister and sphinx because if I see her again I might actually turn furry frfr), I can rightfully say that Dragon's Dogma II is a great game beyond my initial impression.

Background: I've played DDDA for a long while and have completed it many times. I have seen many Arisens sat on that Seneschal throne many times and have heard dear Olra scream in pain as she was reduced to ashes because Damian can't say a proper sentence. BUT what I love about that game is not primarily the combat but the story. I know, controversial.

That's why I can rightfully say I was wrong about DD2. I thought it would be just like DDDA but completed. Instead, they still didn't make us go to the moon but at least we have cat people now which is great (tangentially, whenever I see them there's an echo in my head from somewhere of someone screaming SPLEEEEENNNN and I cringe everytime I do. Some kind of PTSD of sorts, not sure).

But as they say, when things become different, the more they stay the same.

The adventure aspect of Dragon's Dogma was still there. The action combat, the corny dialogues, the convoluted quests (HOW WAS I SUPPOSED TO KNOW TO NOT HELP THE THIEF BRO WTF), the pawn chattering away that seemed delightful and cute at first but if I hear another "This way Arisen. I shall lead you there," I might actually start sacrificing random pawns to the Brine. And yeah, the story too. I love the story in this one but not as much as the first one.

This one focused more on the political side of stuff. I don't hate it but it certainly does pull away from the focus on you being an Arisen. But what I love about it the most is the second part. It still makes you feel that the entire world hangs on your actions. It still felt like you are the anchor to which the world was, ahem, moored. And the ending was great. Not as great as stabbing yourself in the heart and having your main pawn replacing you in the world but it was great nonetheless. The only other criticism I have about the story is the lack of personal movements in peak times such as the time when I was trapped in the Brine and had to swat away at phantoms. I wish I was doing the swatting (punching) like in DD1 where you had to abandon every relationship you had with humans to become essentially god (with a lower g).

I guess what I'm trying to say is Dragon's Dogma 2 is what not what I expected but it was what I came to love.
